lines.text: The peace talks were held in a white tent on a sandbar in the middle of the river. Neutral ground, they called it. It was mostly mud.
My father sat on one side. Lady Sabine Corrow sat on the other. And I sat in the corner, where my father had told me to sit, and say nothing.
House Corrow withdraws its claim to the River Senn. For one generation.
Forever. And reparations, for the villages you burned on our side of the river.
Forever is a very long time, Lord Varr.
So is starving. Your army has eaten its horses.
She signed. Her hand did not shake once. Then she looked past my father, straight at me.
The second son. The zero. I laughed at you once, in your father's hall. Do you remember?
I remember.
I won't make that mistake twice.
She smiled as she said it. It was the most frightening thing I saw in the whole war.
That evening, the camp celebrated. Every soldier, every knight, every lord. Except one.
You! Little brother! You made a fool of me in front of the whole army!
I won your war, Maric. You're welcome.
You won nothing. You hid behind farmers and a ditch. A Varr settles honour with steel. I challenge you. Here. Now.
The whole camp went quiet. A five-ring lord, challenging a zero to a duel. Everyone knew how that ended.
The law allows a lord to name a champion. I name Sir Oswin Hale.
A drunk? A disgraced drunk? Fine. I'll beat him first, and then you.
My lord. He has five rings. I have three. Or I had three, last time anyone checked.
When did anyone last check?
...Before Greyhollow.
Maric attacked like a storm. Fire burst along his blade. Ember aether, the pride of House Varr. The first blow knocked Oswin back three paces.
The second blow didn't.
Frost spread along Oswin's sword. Thick, white, and cold enough to hiss against my brother's fire.
Rime aether? At that strength? You're a three-ring nobody!
I was.
Three strokes later, my brother was flat on his back in the mud, with a frozen blade at his throat.
Now can I shoot him?
Still no.
Maric got up without a word. He didn't look at Oswin. He looked at me. And for the first time in my life, my brother looked afraid.
Behind the crowd, unnoticed, my father watched. He wasn't smiling. He looked like a man watching a storm come in from the sea.
The Lord Who Measured Zero. Chapter thirteen, coming soon.
